groups.title: Replication Fundamentals
groups.question: Explain how replication keeps copies of a database in sync.

followUps.Streaming Replication in PostgreSQL: What is the trade-off between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and why should you watch replication lag?
followUps.MongoDB Replica Sets: Why should your app connect with the replica set URI instead of to a single MongoDB server?

evidence.text: Synchronous replication waits for a replica to confirm, so no committed data is lost, but writes are slower and stall if the replica is down.
Asynchronous replication doesn't wait, so it's fast but a failover can lose recent commits.
Watching lag tells you how much data a failover would lose and how stale replica reads are.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (WAL, synchronous, asynchronous) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says asynchronous replication never loses data.

evidence.text: With the replica set URI the driver knows all members and finds the current primary.
After a failover it follows the new primary and retries, instead of failing on a dead server.
Connecting to one server breaks when that server stops being primary.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (replica set, URI) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says connecting to one member is the same as the replica set URI.

groups.title: Sharding & Horizontal Scaling
groups.question: Walk through how you would split data across machines or partitions as it grows.

followUps.Sharding Strategy — Range vs Hash: Compare a range shard key with a hash shard key, and explain why the first choice is so hard to undo.
followUps.PostgreSQL Table Partitioning: How does partition pruning work, and what kind of query loses its benefit?

evidence.text: A range key keeps related ranges together, good for range queries, but new writes pile onto one hot shard.
A hash key spreads writes evenly, but range queries must ask every shard.
Changing the key means moving all the data, so the first choice is hard to undo.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (shard key, range, hash) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the shard key can be changed any time at no cost.

evidence.text: Partitioning splits one table into child tables by a key like date.
A query that filters on the partition key only scans the matching partitions.
A query without the partition key in its filter has to scan every partition.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (partitioning, pruning) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says partitioning speeds up every query.

groups.title: High Availability & Failover
groups.question: Explain how a database setup stays available when a server or the network fails.

followUps.CAP Theorem & Consistency Models: During a network split, what does a database have to choose between, and how does that map to sync and async replication?
followUps.Patroni & Automatic Failover for Postgre: How does a tool like Patroni promote a new primary, and why is split brain so dangerous?

evidence.text: During a network split a system must choose consistency or availability.
Synchronous replication chooses consistency: writes wait or fail.
Asynchronous replication chooses availability: writes continue but replicas can diverge.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CAP) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a system can keep full consistency and availability during a partition.

evidence.text: Patroni uses a consensus store (etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper) to agree which node is primary.
When the primary fails it promotes a standby and repoints the others.
Split brain, two primaries accepting writes, creates conflicting data that is very hard to merge.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Patroni, failover) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says manual promotion is just as fast and safe.

groups.title: Redis Cluster
groups.question: Walk through how you would scale reads and keep Redis available as load grows.

followUps.Redis Sentinel vs Redis Cluster: When would you pick Redis Cluster over Sentinel, and when is Cluster overkill?
followUps.Read Replicas & Load Balancing: A user updates their profile but still sees old data on the next page. How can read replicas cause that, and how do you fix it?

evidence.text: Sentinel gives failover, but all data still fits on one primary.
Cluster shards data across nodes by hash slots, scaling memory and writes.
Cluster is overkill when the data fits on one node, and it limits multi-key operations.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Sentinel, Redis Cluster) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says Sentinel and Cluster both shard data.

evidence.text: Replicas apply changes a little later than the primary.
A read right after a write can hit a replica that hasn't caught up.
Send reads that need fresh data (like just after your own write) to the primary, or wait for the replica.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (read replica, replication lag) without explaining how they work or why they matter.
